newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - WINTERTHUR. AVIATION BROKERS.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - WINTERTHUR. AVIATION BROKERS.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Swiss insurance group Winterthur said on Tuesday its profits in France were up to 78.9 million francs in 1996 compared with 64.4 million in 1995. Winterthur Assurances said 69.2 million francs came from non-life and 9.7 million from life business.
The announcement appears to indicate further success in the Swiss company's efforts to make money in a market which has been notoriously difficult for foreign firms.
Because Switzerland is relatively small, Winterthur like Zurich Insurance has to look elsewhere for additional core markets. Last year it decided to make greater efforts in France.

In a restructure of its life operation last summer Winterthur decided to segment and regionalise its clientele of private persons to renew its portfolio, and reinforce its activity with the small and medium companies.

Thanks to the restarting market and to a plan to revamp its activity, the French subsidiary of the Swiss insurer returned to profits last year one year ahead of target. This weeks figures indicate that Winterthur is capitalising in the gain. With the French market becoming increasingly lively as privatisation continues, that is a useful position to be in.
--OO0OO--

Aviation brokers were in defensive mood at an airline insurance conference in London this week. Bigger airlines are increasingly retaining more risk themselves or turning to captive insurers. Competition is intense and margins are under pressure.

Against this grim background, speakers addressing the conference highlighted the opportunities presented by these challenges, especially for brokers who are prepared to develop new skills and value added services.
On the traditional side, airlines, especially the smaller ones, will continue to need a go-between who acts in their interests when negotiating with insurers and hunts down the best deals.
However, relying on arranging basic hull and liability cover from conventional underwriters is unlikely to provide a long-term future for most aviation brokers.

To ensure their survival, brokers will have to widen their activities and expand their horizons beyond the London market. In particular, they will have to scour global markets for the growing range of alternative risk transfer mechanisms, such as catastrophe bonds and derivatives.
In a market which is set to grow for some time, innovative brokers do have a future, but only if they evolve to meet the changing demands of airlines.
--OO0OO--
